newsitem.title: CANADA: Alliance Forest sees '97 profit below '96.
newsitem.headline: Alliance Forest sees '97 profit below '96.

text.p: Alliance Forest Products Inc expects its 1997 profit to be below 1996 earnings, mainly because of lower newsprint prices, company officials said on Wednesday.
"I am not expecting us to match the profits realized in 1996," Pierre Monahan, president and chief executive officer said after the company's annual meeting.
That means profits at Alliance Forest would decline for the third consecutive year since the company was created in 1994 through a spinoff of two newsprint mills from Domtar Inc .
In 1996, Alliance Forest had a net profit of C$56 million or C$3.21 a share, versus a profit of C$81.2 million or C$4.56 a share in 1995.
Alliance Forest's first-quarter 1997 profit plunged to C$900,000 or C$0.05 a share from C$C$20.6 million or C$1.18 a share in the year earlier quarter, mainly because of lower newsprint prices.
Eastern North American newsprint prices were about US$500 a tonne at the beginning of 1997, compared with US$700 a tonne in early 1996, Monahan said. He expects newsprint prices to rally this year.
A US$75-a-tonne increase in newsprint prices announced by most producers for this month is expected to stick, Monahan said. The increase had been postponed from February and March.
A rebound in newsprint prices and stable lumber prices would translate into stronger profits in the second half of the year, Monahan said.
"If we isolate the second half of this year, we should beat our second-half 1996 profit," he said.

Alliance Forest is the fourth-largest lumber producer in eastern Canada. Monahan said he expects the North American lumber market to remain strong until June at least, and to be "acceptable" for the second half of the year.

Industry officials had been fearful that because the new fiscal year for the Canada-U.S. agreement regarding quotas on Canadian lumber exports to the United States began April 1, some producers would hold back shipments until that date to avoid paying duties on over-shipments for the year ending March 31.
That would have resulted in a flood of Canadian lumber in the first quarter of the agreement's new fiscal year and a plunge in lumber prices.
"The good news is that was not the case. There is no (lumber) inventory in the pipeline, and on April 1, on the contrary, prices rose," Monahan said.
Monahan said Alliance Forest's US$600 million acquisition of the Coosa Pines pulp and paper operations of Kimberly-Clark Corp in Alabama will be "accretive" to the company's earnings in 1997.
The acquisition, announced in December, closed on March 27. Coosa Pines' results will be fully integrated into Alliance Forest's results beginning April 1.
With Coosa Pines, half of Alliance Forest's revenues will come from newsprint and uncoated groundwood papers, while pulp and lumber will account for 25 percent each of total sales.
Monahan said the company is planning no further acquisitions this year, and is not interested in the assets of Repap Enterprises Inc.
